title: Hippocrene. Pierides
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Minerva has been travelling as her brother's companion; here she leaves him and goes alone to Helicon, the mountain of the Muses, to see a spring that a horse's hoof struck out of the rock. The Muses show her the water and make her welcome — and then, because a goddess is standing in front of them, tell her what they are still afraid of: a king who offered them shelter from a storm and bolted the doors behind them. That story is interrupted by nine magpies calling from the branches overhead, and the interruption turns into a second story — nine sisters who challenged the nine Muses to a singing match, and what the challenger sang when she went first. The part ends at the moment Calliope stands up to answer, with the answer still to come. The Latin is dactylic hexameter, and the sentences run freely across the verse lines, so the unit you tap usually spans two or three of them; the line numbers are the standard way of citing the poem. There is no text-to-speech for Latin here — reading is by eye.

advisory.lede: This part contains an attempted rape: a king shuts the Muses inside his house in order to force them, and they get out only by taking wing.
advisory.more: The Muses' account of Pyreneus runs from line 276 to line 293. He offers them shelter from a storm, closes his doors once they are inside, and 'vim parat' — 'readies force', the ordinary Latin phrase for violence done to a person, and here for rape. They escape by putting on wings; he climbs a tower to follow them, throws himself off and dies. The telling is brief and glancing, and the escape is complete, but the Muse who tells it says she has not got her wits back yet. The text is presented as written, and the translation says what the Latin says rather than softening it.

sentences.t:
Hactenus aurigenae comitem Tritonia fratri
se dedit:
sentences.l:
Thus far, as companion to her gold-born brother, Tritonia
gave herself:
sentences.i: So far Tritonia had gone as her brother's companion — the brother begotten in a shower of gold.
sentences.n: 'Hactenus' — 'up to this point' — is a seam-word: it closes off what came before and turns the poem to something new. 'Tritonia' is one of the goddess's cult names, and this part will call her several different things before it ends. 'aurigenae' ('gold-begotten') agrees with 'fratri' and is a compound of the kind epic likes: the brother's father came to his mother as a shower of gold, which makes him the goddess's half-brother. 'comitem' is a predicate accusative with 'se dedit' — 'gave herself as a companion', not 'gave a companion'.

sentences.t:
inde cava circumdata nube Seriphon
deserit, a dextra Cythno Gyaroque relictis,
quaque super pontum via visa brevissima, Thebas
virgineumque Helicona petit.
sentences.l:
thence, wrapped about in a hollow cloud, Seriphos
she leaves, Cythnos and Gyaros left on the right,
and where over the sea the way looked shortest, Thebes
and maiden Helicon she seeks.
sentences.i: From there she left Seriphos behind, wrapped in a hollow cloud, keeping Cythnos and Gyaros to her right, and took the shortest crossing she could see over the sea, making for Thebes and virgin Helicon.
sentences.n: 'circumdata' is a passive participle used in the middle sense — she has put the cloud round herself, not had it put round her — and 'cava nube' is the ablative that goes with it. 'a dextra Cythno Gyaroque relictis' is an ablative absolute: a small self-contained clause, 'with Cythnos and Gyaros left to starboard', where English wants 'once she had left them'. You will meet several more in this part. 'quaque' is 'qua' plus the joining '-que' — 'and by the route where…' — not any form of 'quisque'; that split is worth watching for every time you see a word ending in '-que'. Seriphos, Cythnos and Gyaros are islands of the Cyclades; Helicon is the Muses' mountain in Boeotia, near Thebes, and 'virgineum' ('maiden') marks it as theirs.

sentences.t:
Quo monte potita
constitit et doctas sic est adfata sorores:
sentences.l:
Having taken possession of that mountain,
she halted, and thus addressed the learned sisters:
sentences.i: Once she had the mountain under her, she stopped, and spoke to the learned sisters like this:
sentences.n: 'Quo' is a connecting relative — a relative pronoun opening a new sentence, which English turns into 'and that…' or simply 'that…'. 'quo monte' is ablative because 'potior' ('take possession of') governs the ablative rather than the accusative. 'doctas sorores', the 'learned sisters', are the Muses. 'adfata est' is the edition's spelling (not 'affata') and the verb is deponent: passive in form, active in sense.

sentences.t:
“Fama novi fontis nostras pervenit ad aures,
dura Medusaei quem praepetis ungula rupit.
sentences.l:
'Report of a new spring has come through to our ears,
which the hard hoof of the Medusa-born swift-flier broke open.
sentences.i: 'Word of a new spring has reached my ears — one that the hard hoof of Medusa's winged horse burst open.
sentences.n: 'nostras … aures' is a poetic plural for 'my ears': a god speaking of herself often says 'we'. 'quem' looks back across the line-end to 'fontis', the spring — Latin verse routinely holds a relative pronoun until it is well inside its own clause, and here it is the third word of its own line. 'Medusaei praepetis' is a periphrasis rather than a name: 'the Medusaean swift-flier', the horse who sprang from Medusa. 'praepes' is properly an adjective, 'swift on the wing', used here as a noun. 'rupit' is strong — 'burst, broke open' — so the water is not found but made.

sentences.t:
Is mihi causa viae. Volui mirabile factum
cernere: vidi ipsum materno sanguine nasci.”
sentences.l:
That is the reason of the journey for me. I wished the marvellous event
to see: I saw him himself be born from his mother's blood.'
sentences.i: That is why I have come. I wanted to see the marvel for myself — and I did see him born, out of his mother's blood.'
sentences.n: 'Is … causa viae' has no verb at all: Latin drops 'est' freely and English has to put it back. 'mihi' is a dative of possession — 'the reason of the journey is to me' = 'my reason for coming'. 'factum' here is not a deed done by anyone but the thing that happened, the marvel itself. 'vidi ipsum … nasci' is accusative and infinitive after a verb of perceiving: 'I saw him be born'. 'materno sanguine' is the blood of the horse's mother, the Gorgon, and the speaker says plainly that she was standing there when it happened.

sentences.t:
Excipit Uranie: “Quaecumque est causa videndi
has tibi, diva, domos, animo gratissima nostro es.
sentences.l:
Urania takes it up: 'Whatever is the reason of seeing
these halls for you, goddess, most welcome to our heart you are.
sentences.i: Urania picked up the word: 'Whatever brought you to see this house, goddess, you could not be more welcome to us.
sentences.n: 'Excipit' — 'takes up' — is the ordinary verb for answering, catching another speaker's thread. It is a present tense among past ones: the historic present, which quickens the scene, and which you will see again several times in this part. 'causa videndi has … domos' is a gerund keeping its own accusative object, 'has domos' — strict prose would recast this as a gerundive, but verse allows it. 'animo … nostro' is a dative with 'gratissima': 'most pleasing to our heart'. Urania is one of the nine.

sentences.t:
Vera tamen fama est, et Pegasus huius origo
fontis”, et ad latices deduxit Pallada sacros.
sentences.l:
True, though, the report is, and Pegasus is the origin of this
spring' — and she led Pallas to the sacred waters.
sentences.i: But the report is true: Pegasus is where this spring comes from' — and she led Pallas over to the sacred water.
sentences.n: 'huius origo / fontis' is stretched across the line-end — 'the origin of this … spring' — and has no verb of its own, so English supplies 'is'. The quotation closes in mid-line and the narrative picks up in the same breath, without so much as a new sentence. 'Pallada' is a Greek accusative of 'Pallas': Greek names keep their Greek endings in Latin verse, and this is the same goddess called 'Tritonia' at 250. 'ad latices … sacros' is wrapped round the verb, which is how a Latin line often frames its own centre.

sentences.t:
Quae mirata diu factas pedis ictibus undas,
silvarum lucos circumspicit antiquarum
antraque et innumeris distinctas floribus herbas
felicesque vocat pariter studioque locoque
Mnemonidas.
sentences.l:
And she, having marvelled long at the waters made by the blows of a hoof,
looks round at the groves of ancient
woods, and the caves, and the grasses picked out with countless
flowers, and calls happy, alike in their pursuit and their place,
the daughters of Mnemosyne.
sentences.i: She gazed a long while at water struck out of the ground by a hoof, then looked about her at the groves of the old woods, the caves, the grass embroidered with flowers past counting — and told the daughters of Mnemosyne how lucky they were, in their calling and in their home alike.
sentences.n: 'Quae' is another connecting relative: 'and she'. 'mirata' is deponent and active in sense, 'having marvelled'. 'pedis ictibus' — 'by the blows of a foot' — is the hoof of the horse named at 262. Two phrases are wrapped right round their own nouns here, 'silvarum … antiquarum' round 'lucos' and 'innumeris … floribus' round 'distinctas'; that interlocking order (hyperbaton) is the sound of the description opening out. 'felices … vocat … Mnemonidas' is a double accusative — to call somebody something. 'Mnemonidas' is a Greek accusative plural, 'the daughters of Mnemosyne' (Memory): the Muses again, under a third name.

sentences.t: Quam sic adfata est una sororum:
sentences.l: Her one of the sisters thus addressed:
sentences.i: One of the sisters answered her like this:
sentences.n: 'Quam' is the third connecting relative in a few lines — 'and her'. Latin habitually joins one sentence to the next with a relative pronoun where English would start fresh with a plain pronoun. 'una sororum' leaves the speaker unnamed, and she stays unnamed through the whole long speech that follows.

sentences.t:
“O, nisi te virtus opera ad maiora tulisset,
in partem ventura chori Tritonia nostri,
vera refers meritoque probas artesque locumque,
et gratam sortem, tutae modo simus, habemus.
sentences.l:
'O, had valour not carried you off to greater works,
one to come into a share of our chorus, Tritonia,
you report true things, and deservedly you approve both our arts and our place,
and a welcome lot we have — if only we be safe.
sentences.i: 'Tritonia — you would have joined our company yourself, if your courage had not carried you off to greater work — what you say is true, and you are right to think well of our art and our home; ours is a happy lot, if only we could be safe in it.
sentences.n: 'ventura' is a future participle doing the work of an unreal conditional: 'you who were going to come into a share of our chorus' = 'you who would have joined us', if the 'nisi' clause were not true. 'tulisset' is pluperfect subjunctive, the regular mark of a condition contrary to fact. 'artesque locumque' is the correlative '-que … -que', 'both … and', a pairing that belongs to verse rather than prose. 'tutae modo simus' is a proviso clause — 'modo' with the subjunctive, 'provided only that we be safe' — and it turns the compliment sour in mid-sentence, which is what sets up the story coming next.

sentences.t:
Sed (vetitum est adeo sceleri nihil) omnia terrent
virgineas mentes, dirusque ante ora Pyreneus
vertitur, et nondum tota me mente recepi.
sentences.l:
But — so completely is nothing forbidden to crime — everything frightens
maiden minds, and dreadful Pyreneus before our faces
keeps turning, and not yet with my whole mind have I recovered myself.
sentences.i: But everything frightens a girl's mind — there is nothing at all that crime is held back from — and dreadful Pyreneus keeps moving there in front of our eyes; even now I have not got my wits fully back.
sentences.n: The brackets are the edition's punctuation of an aside: 'vetitum est adeo sceleri nihil', word for word 'nothing at all is forbidden to crime', with 'sceleri' dative — her reason for saying the fear is reasonable. 'virgineas mentes' is the object of 'terrent', not a possessive: 'everything frightens maiden minds'. 'vertitur' is present, and the present is the whole point — the man is dead, and he is still turning there in front of her. 'tota me mente recepi' — 'I have recovered myself with my whole mind' — is the idiom for getting one's wits back.

sentences.t:
Daulida Threicio Phoceaque milite rura
ceperat ille ferox iniustaque regna tenebat.
sentences.l:
Daulis and the Phocian country, with Thracian soldiery,
that fierce man had seized, and was holding an unjust rule.
sentences.i: That savage had taken Daulis and the countryside of Phocis with Thracian troops, and was holding a kingdom he had no right to.
sentences.n: 'Daulida' is a Greek accusative singular: Daulis, a town of Phocis in central Greece, under Parnassus. 'Threicio … milite' is a collective singular — one 'soldier' standing for a whole army, which Latin does readily and English cannot. The two verbs are pluperfect and imperfect: the seizing is finished, the occupation is still going on when the story opens. 'ille ferox' is held back to the second line, so the sentence names everything he took before it names him.

sentences.t: Templa petebamus Parnasia: vidit euntes,
sentences.l: We were making for the Parnasian temples: he saw us going,
sentences.i: We were on our way to the temples on Parnassus, and he saw us pass,
sentences.n: 'petebamus' is imperfect — an action still under way when his eye catches it. 'euntes' is the participle of 'eo' (go), accusative plural, with 'nos' left to be understood: 'saw [us] going'. The Parnasian temples are those on the slopes of Parnassus, in the very country he has just been said to hold.

sentences.t:
nostraque fallaci veneratus numina vultu
“Mnemonides” (cognorat enim), “consistite” dixit,
“nec dubitate, precor, tecto grave sidus et imbrem”
(imber erat) “vitare meo:
sentences.l:
and, having done reverence to our godhead with a lying face,
'Mnemonides' — for he had recognised us — 'halt,' he said,
'and do not hesitate, I beg, the heavy weather and the rain'
(it was raining) 'to escape under my roof:
sentences.i: and, paying our godhead a show of reverence with a false face, he said: 'Mnemonides' — he had recognised us — 'stop here; do not be shy, I beg you, of getting out of this foul weather and the rain under my roof' — and it was in fact raining —
sentences.n: 'veneratus' is deponent, active in sense in spite of its passive shape: 'having paid reverence'. 'fallaci … vultu' is the ablative of the means he did it with. 'cognorat' is a contracted 'cognoverat' ('he had recognised'), the sort of syncopation verse uses freely. 'grave sidus' is literally 'a heavy star' — a constellation whose rising was held to bring bad weather, so simply 'foul weather'. Note where the aside falls: the ablative 'tecto … meo' ('under my roof') is split clean across '(imber erat)', the narrating Muse breaking into her own quotation of him to confirm that his pretext was at least true. 'nec dubitate … vitare' is 'do not hesitate to escape', with the infinitive held back across the aside into the next line.

sentences.t:
subiere minores
saepe casas superi.”
sentences.l:
the gods above have often gone in under
smaller cottages [than this].'
sentences.i: 'gods have often gone in under a poorer roof than mine.'
sentences.n: 'subiere' is the poetic third-person plural perfect in '-ēre', short for 'subierunt' ('they have gone under'). It is everywhere in verse, and you will meet it twice more in this part. 'minores … casas' is the object of 'subiere' ('go under' takes an accusative in Latin), and 'casa' is a hut or cottage, chosen to be humble; the comparative 'minores' leaves the comparison unspoken — smaller than his own house. 'superi', 'those above', is a standard word for the gods. He is flattering them with a piety he does not have.

sentences.t:
Dictis et tempore motae
adnuimusque viro primasque intravimus aedes.
sentences.l:
Moved by his words and by the weather,
we both consented to the man and entered the outer rooms.
sentences.i: His words and the weather moved us: we said yes to him, and stepped into the front of the house.
sentences.n: 'motae' is feminine plural — the speaker is including herself and her sisters, and Latin marks their gender in the participle where English has no way to. 'dictis et tempore' is ablative of cause, and 'tempus' here is the weather, the moment as it stood. 'adnuimusque … primasque' is the correlative '-que … -que', 'both … and'. 'primas aedes' is the front part of a house, the rooms just inside the door: they go no further than that, and the word matters for what happens next.

sentences.t:
Desierant imbres, victoque aquilonibus austro
fusca repurgato fugiebant nubila caelo.
sentences.l:
The rains had ceased, and, the south wind conquered by the north winds,
the dark clouds were fleeing, the sky swept clean.
sentences.i: The rain had stopped; the north winds had beaten the south wind down, and the dark clouds were streaming away from a sky wiped clear.
sentences.n: Two ablative absolutes in a single sentence: 'victo aquilonibus austro' ('with the south wind beaten by the north winds') and 'repurgato … caelo' ('with the sky scoured out again'). Each is a compact clause of its own that English has to unfold into a full one. Auster is the rain-bringing south wind, Aquilo the cold north wind that clears the sky after it. 'fusca … nubila' is the subject, split round its verb; 'fugiebant' is imperfect, so the clouds are still going as she describes them — the storm is over and the excuse for staying has gone with it.

sentences.t:
Impetus ire fuit: claudit sua tecta Pyreneus
vimque parat.
sentences.l:
There was an urge to go: Pyreneus shuts his house
and makes ready force.
sentences.i: We were minded to leave — and Pyreneus shut the house up and set about taking us by force.
sentences.n: 'Impetus ire fuit' is very compressed: 'there was an urge to go', a bare infinitive hanging on a noun, which is verse licence. Then the tenses change: 'claudit … parat' are presents among perfects and imperfects, the historic present snapping the narrative into the moment the trap closes. 'vim parare' is 'to make force ready'; 'vis' is the ordinary Latin word for violence done to a person, and here it means rape, which is what he shut the doors in order to do.

sentences.t: Quam nos sumptis effugimus alis.
sentences.l: Which we escaped, our wings taken up.
sentences.i: We took wing and got away from it.
sentences.n: 'Quam' is a connecting relative picking up 'vim', 'force', from the line before — 'and this we escaped'. 'sumptis … alis' is another ablative absolute, 'with wings taken up': the wings are something the Muses put on and take off at will. Set that against the birds at 298–301 in this same part, whose wings were not their own idea.

sentences.t:
Ipse secuturo similis stetit arduus arce
“qua” que “via est vobis, erit et mihi” dixit “eadem”,
sentences.l:
He himself, like one about to follow, stood towering on the citadel,
'and by whatever road there is for you,' he said, 'the same will be for me too,'
sentences.i: He himself stood high on the citadel like a man about to come after us, and said, 'whatever road is yours, that same road will be mine as well,'
sentences.n: 'secuturo similis' — 'similis' with the dative of a future participle, 'like one who is going to follow'. 'arduus' describes the man, not the citadel: he stood there steep and high. In the second line the edition prints the joining '-que' outside the quotation marks, because the enclitic belongs to the narrator's sentence while the word it hangs on begins his speech; read the two together as one word, 'quaque', the same 'qua-que' you met at 253. 'vobis' and 'mihi' are datives of possession: 'the road that is to you … will be to me as well'.

sentences.t:
seque iacit vecors e summae culmine turris
et cadit in vultus, discussisque ossibus oris
tundit humum moriens scelerato sanguine tinctam.”
sentences.l:
and out of his mind he throws himself from the top of the highest tower
and falls upon his face, and, the bones of his face struck apart,
dying he beats the ground, stained with his accursed blood.'
sentences.i: and out of his senses he threw himself from the top of the high tower and came down on his face; the bones of it smashed, he lay dying and drumming on ground his own foul blood had dyed.'
sentences.n: 'seque iacit' keeps the historic present running to the last verb of the story. 'vecors' — 'out of one's wits' — is dropped in right beside the verb, and it is the word the whole action turns on. 'discussis … ossibus oris' is an ablative absolute again, 'the bones of his face having been struck apart'; 'os, oris' here is the face, not the mouth. 'scelerato sanguine tinctam' agrees with 'humum', the ground: it is the earth that is dyed, and 'sceleratus' ('criminal, accursed') puts the verdict on the blood itself. The Muse's account of Pyreneus ends here, in mid-line.

sentences.t:
Musa loquebatur: pennae sonuere per auras,
voxque salutantum ramis veniebat ab altis.
sentences.l:
The Muse was speaking: wings sounded through the air,
and a voice of greeters was coming from the high branches.
sentences.i: The Muse was still speaking when wings whirred through the air, and a voice of creatures calling a greeting came down out of the high branches.
sentences.n: 'loquebatur' is imperfect — she is in mid-speech when the interruption comes, and the tense is what tells you she never finishes. 'sonuere' is the poetic third-plural perfect for 'sonuerunt'; you met the same ending in 'subiere' at 282. 'salutantum' is a contracted 'salutantium', genitive plural of the participle: 'of creatures greeting [her]'. The sentence gives the sound first and the cause much later, so the reader stays in the dark exactly as long as the goddess does.

sentences.t:
Suspicit et linguae quaerit tam certa loquentes
unde sonent hominemque putat Iove nata locutum:
sentences.l:
She looks up, and asks whence tongues speaking things so distinct
sound; and she who was born of Jove thinks that a human has spoken:
sentences.i: She looked up and asked where tongues speaking so plainly could be sounding from; Jove's daughter took it for a human voice.
sentences.n: 'quaerit … unde sonent' is an indirect question, which is why 'sonent' is subjunctive; the whole phrase 'linguae … tam certa loquentes' is pulled out in front of its own 'unde'. 'tam certa' is neuter plural, the object of 'loquentes': 'speaking things so definite', that is, articulate words and not bird-noise. 'Iove nata' — 'born of Jove' — names the goddess by her descent instead of her name; she is 'Tritonia' at 250 and 270, and 'Pallas' at 336 and in its Greek accusative 'Pallada' at 263. 'hominem … locutum [esse]' is accusative and infinitive after 'putat', with 'esse' left out as it usually is.

sentences.t:
Ales erat, numeroque novem, sua fata querentes,
institerant ramis imitantes omnia picae.
sentences.l:
It was a bird; and, nine in number, lamenting their own fates,
they had settled on the branches, imitating everything — magpies.
sentences.i: It was a bird. Nine of them had settled on the branches, complaining of their fate and copying whatever they heard: magpies.
sentences.n: The answer is held back to the last word of the sentence — 'picae', magpies — and 'Ales erat' answers the question of the line before in two words: not a person, a bird. 'numero novem' is an ablative of respect, 'nine as to number'. 'querentes' and 'imitantes' are both nominative plural, agreeing with a 'picae' that only arrives across the line-end. 'imitantes omnia' — 'imitating everything' — is what magpies were proverbially for, and the nine whose story follows are the ones who set out to match the Muses at their own art.

sentences.t:
Miranti sic orsa deae dea: “Nuper et istae
auxerunt volucrum victae certamine turbam.
sentences.l:
To the wondering goddess the goddess thus began: 'Lately these too,
beaten in a contest, swelled the crowd of birds.
sentences.i: Goddess to wondering goddess, she began: 'Those creatures swelled the flock of birds too, and not long ago — they lost a contest.
sentences.n: 'Miranti … deae dea' sets the two of them side by side inside one line: the dative 'miranti … deae' is the goddess listening in wonder, and the nominative 'dea' is the Muse who speaks. 'orsa [est]' is deponent — 'she began' — with 'est' understood. 'istae' is the demonstrative of the second person, 'those there by you', and in this speaker's mouth it keeps its distance: they are her rivals, and the word is hers, not the poem's. 'victae' is feminine plural agreeing with 'istae': being beaten and becoming birds are the same event.

sentences.t:
Pieros has genuit Pellaeis dives in arvis,
Paeonis Euippe mater fuit.
sentences.l:
Pieros, a rich man, begot these in the Pellaean fields,
Paeonian Euippe was their mother.
sentences.i: Their father was Pieros, a rich man of the fields of Pella; their mother was Euippe of Paeonia.
sentences.n: 'genuit' is the verb used of a father — 'begot' — and the mother gets a clause of her own; a balanced pair of lines like this is the standard Latin way of giving a pedigree. 'Pellaeis in arvis': Pella was the royal city of Macedonia. 'Paeonis' is a Greek feminine adjective, 'the Paeonian woman'; Paeonia lay north of Macedonia, and it comes back at 313 in the challenge itself, where going home means going there.

sentences.t:
Illa potentem
Lucinam noviens, noviens paritura, vocavit.
sentences.l:
She called on powerful
Lucina nine times, nine times about to give birth.
sentences.i: Nine times she called on Lucina in her power — nine times she was to be brought to bed.
sentences.n: Lucina is the goddess called on in childbirth, and 'vocare Lucinam' is simply what a woman in labour does. 'noviens, noviens' is repeated with no connective between (asyndeton), the second one attached to 'paritura', a future participle: 'nine times, and nine times on the point of bearing'. The doubling is the arithmetic the whole story runs on — nine daughters, to set against nine Muses.

sentences.t:
Intumuit numero stolidarum turba sororum,
perque tot Haemonias et per tot Achaidas urbes
huc venit et tali committit proelia voce:
sentences.l:
The crowd of stupid sisters swelled at the number,
and through so many Haemonian and through so many Achaean cities
it comes here, and joins battle with words like these:
sentences.i: That number went to the stupid sisters' heads, and through city after city of Haemonia and Achaea they came all the way here and opened the fight with words like these:
sentences.n: 'Intumuit' is literally 'swelled up' — of a body, of a river, and here of pride. 'numero' is ablative of cause: it is the count of nine that puffs them up. 'turba … sororum' is grammatically singular, so the Latin verbs stay singular where English has to say 'they'. 'stolidarum' — 'dull, thick-headed' — is the narrating Muse's word for her rivals, not a neutral description, and it is worth reading everything that follows as her account. 'venit' is spelled exactly like the perfect 'vēnit' in an edition that marks no vowel lengths; the present 'committit' beside it is why it is taken as a present here. 'committere proelia' is the set phrase for joining battle — the singing match is called a war before a note is sung.

sentences.t:
“Desinite indoctum vana dulcedine vulgus
fallere: nobiscum, siqua est fiducia vobis,
Thespiades certate deae.
sentences.l:
'Stop the unlearned crowd with your empty sweetness
deceiving: with us, if there is any confidence to you,
compete, you Thespian goddesses.
sentences.i: 'Stop cheating the ignorant crowd with that empty sweetness of yours. Take us on, if you have any confidence in yourselves, you goddesses of Thespiae.
sentences.n: 'Desinite … fallere' is 'stop deceiving', with the infinitive kept waiting till the start of the next line. 'indoctum … vulgus' is the object of 'fallere' — the untrained audience the Muses are accused of playing down to. 'siqua est fiducia vobis' is a dative of possession: 'if there is any confidence to you' = 'if you have any', and the edition prints 'siqua' as one word. 'Thespiades … deae' is a vocative with a sneer in it: Thespiae is the small town at the foot of Helicon, so she is calling them local goddesses. The speech drives on imperatives — 'desinite', 'certate', and 'cedite' at 311 — with its futures and subjunctives hung between them.

sentences.t:
Nec voce nec arte
vincemur, totidemque sumus.
sentences.l:
Neither in voice nor in art
shall we be beaten, and we are just as many.
sentences.i: You will not beat us for voice, and you will not beat us for craft, and there are as many of us as there are of you.
sentences.n: 'nec … nec' names the two things a performance can be judged on: 'vox', the voice itself, and 'ars', the skill behind what is sung. Both are ablatives of respect — beaten 'in respect of' voice or art. 'vincemur' is future passive, 'we shall not be beaten'. 'totidem' is 'just as many', and it is the point of the birth-count at 303–304: the challenge is built on a coincidence of number.

sentences.t:
Vel cedite victae
fonte Medusaeo et Hyantea Aganippe,
vel nos Emathiis ad Paeonas usque nivosos
cedamus campis.
sentences.l:
Either withdraw, beaten,
from the Medusaean spring and Hyantean Aganippe,
or let us withdraw from the Emathian plains
all the way to the snowy Paeonians.
sentences.i: Either you give way, beaten, and leave the spring the horse made and Aganippe of the Hyantes — or we give up the plains of Emathia and go right back to the snows of Paeonia.
sentences.n: 'cedere' with a bare ablative is 'to withdraw from' a place, so 'fonte … Aganippe … campis' are ablatives of separation, not instruments. 'fonte Medusaeo' is the spring of 256–257, named after the horse who opened it; Aganippe is Helicon's other spring, called 'Hyantean' after the old Boeotian people. The stakes are made symmetrical on purpose: whoever loses leaves home. Where the edition prints 'cedamus' ('let us withdraw'), some editions print 'cedemus', 'we shall withdraw'.

sentences.t: Dirimant certamina nymphae.”
sentences.l: Let the nymphs decide the contests.'
sentences.i: Let nymphs settle the match.'
sentences.n: 'Dirimant' is a jussive subjunctive — a command in the third person, 'let them decide'. 'dirimere' is to pull something apart, hence to settle a quarrel by separating the parties. 'certamina' is a poetic plural for the single contest at issue. She names the judges herself, inside her own challenge, before the Muses have said a word.

sentences.t:
Turpe quidem contendere erat, sed cedere visum
turpius.
sentences.l:
It was shameful, indeed, to compete; but to yield seemed
more shameful.
sentences.i: It was degrading to compete — and backing down looked more degrading still.
sentences.n: Two infinitives are being used as subjects — 'contendere' and 'cedere', 'competing' and 'yielding' — with the neuter adjectives 'turpe' and 'turpius' as their predicates. 'visum [est]' drops the verb 'to be', as Latin constantly does. The comparative is left to stand alone at the head of the next line, which is where the weight of the judgment lands. The narrating Muse is admitting that her own side had no good option.

sentences.t:
Electae iurant per flumina nymphae
factaque de vivo pressere sedilia saxo.
sentences.l:
The chosen nymphs swear by the rivers
and pressed seats made out of the living rock.
sentences.i: Nymphs were chosen; they swore by their rivers, and took their seats, cut out of the living rock.
sentences.n: 'iurant' is present and 'pressere' perfect inside one sentence — the tense slides from one to the other, which Latin verse allows and which keeps the scene from settling. 'pressere' is '-ēre' for '-ērunt' again ('they pressed'), the third instance in this part after 'subiere' and 'sonuere'. 'premere sedilia' — 'to press seats' — is the ordinary idiom for sitting down on them. 'vivo … saxo' is 'living rock', stone still in its own bed and not quarried and carried in. Swearing by the rivers is the most binding oath a nymph has to give; 'electae' ('chosen') leaves it unsaid who chose them.

sentences.i: Then, with no lots drawn, the one who had put herself forward first sang the wars of the gods: she set the Giants in a place of honour they had not earned, and made the deeds of the great gods look small.
sentences.n: 'sine sorte' — without casting lots for the running order, which is the fair way and which she simply skips. 'quae se certare professa est' uses the deponent 'profiteri' with accusative and infinitive: 'declared herself to compete'. 'bella … superum': 'superum' is the contracted genitive plural for 'superorum', 'of the gods above'. 'Gigantas' is a Greek accusative plural. 'falso in honore ponit' is 'places them in a false honour' — gives them a glory the song has no right to give — and 'extenuat' is literally 'thins out', makes less of. The charge against her song is that it has the two sides the wrong way round.

sentences.t:
emissumque ima de sede Typhoea terrae
caelitibus fecisse metum cunctosque dedisse
terga fugae, donec fessos Aegyptia tellus
ceperit et septem discretus in ostia Nilus.
sentences.l:
and [she sings] that Typhoeus, sent out from the lowest seat of earth,
made fear for the sky-dwellers, and that they all gave
their backs to flight, until the Egyptian land took them in, weary,
and the Nile, parted into seven mouths.
sentences.i: and she sang that Typhoeus, let loose from the depths of the earth, put fear into the gods of the sky, and that every one of them turned tail and ran, until the land of Egypt took them in exhausted, and the Nile, split into its seven mouths.
sentences.n: The sentence turns into indirect statement without repeating any verb of speaking: 'canit' from the lines above is still governing, and 'Typhoea … fecisse … dedisse' is accusative and infinitive. 'Typhoea' is a Greek accusative singular. 'terga dare fugae' — 'to give one's back to flight' — is the standard Latin idiom for running away, and it is a humiliating one, which is precisely her purpose. 'donec … ceperit' is perfect subjunctive, the mood a 'donec' clause takes once it is reported inside somebody else's words. 'discretus in ostia' is the Nile 'separated into mouths' — the delta.

sentences.t:
Huc quoque terrigenam venisse Typhoea narrat
et se mentitis superos celasse figuris;
sentences.l:
That earth-born Typhoeus came here too she tells,
and that the gods above hid themselves in feigned shapes;
sentences.i: She tells how the earth-born Typhoeus came here as well, and how the gods hid themselves away inside shapes that were lies;
sentences.n: 'quoque' here really is the adverb 'too' (going with 'huc', 'here as well') and not the split 'qua-que' you met at 253 — Latin verse hands you both spellings and only the sense separates them. 'terrigenam', 'earth-born', is a compound of the kind epic likes; Typhoeus was a son of Earth, which is also why he comes 'out of the lowest seat of earth' above. 'se … celasse' is a contracted 'celavisse' in accusative and infinitive, with 'se' pointing back to the gods: they hid themselves. 'mentitis … figuris' is the participle of the deponent 'mentior' pressed into a passive sense, which is the point to watch: the shapes are the thing feigned, not the thing doing the feigning — 'counterfeited shapes'. It sets up the list of animals that follows.

sentences.t:
“duxque gregis” dixit “fit Iuppiter; unde recurvis
nunc quoque formatus Libys est cum cornibus Ammon.
sentences.l:
'and the leader of the flock,' she said, 'Jupiter becomes; from which
even now Libyan Ammon is shaped with curving horns.
sentences.i: 'and Jupiter,' she said, 'turns into the ram that leads the flock; which is why Libyan Ammon is still shown today with horns that curl back.
sentences.n: The narrating Muse now quotes her rival's own words, so this is a quotation inside a quotation; the edition marks both levels the same way, and the 'dixit' dropped into the middle of the line is the only signal that the voice has changed. 'dux gregis' is a periphrasis for the ram. 'fit' is present — the change is told as happening in front of you. 'unde' is 'from which', in the sense 'that is why': the line turns a story into an explanation of a statue people could still go and look at. Ammon was the ram-horned god worshipped in Libya and identified with Jupiter.

sentences.t:
Delius in corvo, proles Semeleia capro,
fele soror Phoebi, nivea Saturnia vacca,
pisce Venus latuit, Cyllenius ibidis alis.”
sentences.l:
The Delian in a raven, Semele's offspring in a goat,
Phoebus's sister in a cat, Saturn's daughter in a snowy cow,
Venus hid in a fish, the Cyllenian in the wings of an ibis.'
sentences.i: Apollo of Delos hid in a raven, Semele's son in a goat, Apollo's sister in a cat, Saturn's daughter in a white cow, Venus in a fish, the god of Cyllene in the wings of an ibis.'
sentences.n: One verb, 'latuit' ('hid'), serves all six clauses, and it is held back to the last line — the whole catalogue hangs on a single word arriving late. Every god is named by a periphrasis rather than by name: 'Delius' is Apollo, born on Delos; 'proles Semeleia' is Bacchus, Semele's child; 'soror Phoebi' is Diana; 'Saturnia' is Juno; 'Cyllenius' is Mercury, born on Mount Cyllene. Only Venus is given her own name, and she gets it in the line that finally supplies the verb. The animals are Egyptian, which is what the flight to Egypt at 323–324 was for.

sentences.t:
Hactenus ad citharam vocalia moverat ora:
poscimur Aonides.
sentences.l:
Thus far to the lyre she had moved her singing mouth:
we Aonides are called for.
sentences.i: That was as far as she took her song to the lyre: then we of Aonia were called on.
sentences.n: 'Hactenus' is the same word this part opened with at 250, doing the same work: it shuts one stretch off and hands over to the next. 'vocalia … ora' is a poetic plural for one singing mouth. 'moverat' is pluperfect, stepping back to round off the rival's performance. 'poscimur' is present passive, first person plural — 'we are being called for', the Muses' turn. 'Aonides' is a nominative plural Greek name for them, from Aonia, the old name for their corner of Boeotia; it stands in apposition to the 'we' buried inside the verb, which is why English has to say 'we Aonides'.

sentences.t:
Sed forsitan otia non sint,
nec nostris praebere vacet tibi cantibus aures.”
sentences.l:
But perhaps there is no leisure,
and it may not be free for you to hold out your ears to our songs.'
sentences.i: But perhaps you have no time to spare, and are not free to give our songs a hearing.'
sentences.n: 'forsitan' ('perhaps') regularly takes the subjunctive, and that is why 'sint' and 'vacet' are subjunctive; the mood is the politeness. She is not saying the goddess is busy — she is offering her a way out. 'vacet' is impersonal, 'there is free time', with 'tibi' the dative of the person who has it. 'praebere aures' — 'to hold out one's ears' — is the ordinary idiom for giving something a hearing. The Muse breaks off her own story to ask leave to go on with it.

sentences.t:
“Ne dubita, vestrumque mihi refer ordine carmen”
Pallas ait nemorisque levi consedit in umbra.
sentences.l:
'Do not hesitate, and report to me your song in order,'
Pallas says, and sat down in the light shade of the grove.
sentences.i: 'Don't hesitate — tell me your song right through,' said Pallas, and settled in the thin shade of the grove.
sentences.n: 'Ne dubita' is a prohibition made with 'ne' and a plain imperative. Prose would say 'noli dubitare'; the short form belongs to verse. 'refer … ordine' is 'report in order' — from the beginning and in sequence, which is what the rest of the episode is going to be. 'ait' is present and 'consedit' perfect within the one sentence, the same slide of tenses as at 316–317. 'levi … umbra' is thin, dappled shade: she is making herself comfortable for a long hearing.

sentences.t: Musa refert: “Dedimus summam certaminis uni.
sentences.l: The Muse reports: 'We gave the whole of the contest to one.
sentences.i: The Muse took it up: 'We put the whole contest into the hands of one of us.
sentences.n: 'refert' answers the 'refer' of 335, two lines above — the goddess asks her to report, and the same verb comes straight back as the narrator's. 'summa certaminis' is 'the sum total of the contest', the whole thing staked on a single performer; 'uni' is the dative of 'unus'. Nine sang against them, and one answers for the nine.

sentences.t:
Surgit et inmissos hedera conlecta capillos
Calliope querulas praetemptat pollice chordas,
atque haec percussis subiungit carmina nervis:
sentences.l:
She rises, and, gathered as to her loosened hair with ivy,
Calliope tries the plaintive strings beforehand with her thumb,
and joins these songs to the struck strings:
sentences.i: Calliope stood up, her loose hair caught back with ivy, ran her thumb over the plaintive strings to try them, and set these songs to the notes she struck:
sentences.n: 'inmissos … capillos' with 'conlecta' is the Greek accusative of respect: the participle is passive in form but reflexive in sense, and the accusative says what part of her it applies to — 'gathered as to her hair', that is, 'having gathered up her hair'. Latin took the construction from Greek and verse uses it constantly; English has to turn it round. 'inmissos' is the edition's spelling of 'immissos', hair 'let go', hanging loose. 'praetemptat' is to try something in advance — she is tuning, testing the strings before she plays them. 'subiungit carmina nervis', 'joins the songs onto the strings', is the last movement before the song itself: the part stops on a colon.

questions: House-rendering candidate, V.315–316 ('Turpe quidem contendere erat, sed cedere visum / turpius'): shipped as literal 'It was shameful, indeed, to compete; but to yield seemed / more shameful' and idiomatic 'It was degrading to compete — and backing down looked more degrading still.' (Review changed the idiomatic: the drafter's 'beneath them' turned a shame word into a question of dignity and moved the Muse's judgement on her own side into the third person.) It is a free-standing sententia a reader may have met quoted on its own, so it should be ratified rather than re-invented in a later part.

House-rendering candidate, V.282–283 ('subiere minores / saepe casas superi'): shipped as literal 'the gods above have often gone in under / smaller cottages [than this]' and idiomatic 'gods have often gone in under a poorer roof than mine.' A quotable tag on hospitality that a reader may have met on its own; added at review because the drafter did not list it.

House-rendering candidate, V.273 ('vetitum est adeo sceleri nihil'): shipped as literal 'so completely is nothing forbidden to crime' and idiomatic 'there is nothing at all that crime is held back from'. A self-contained sententia; added at review.

V.290 ('qua'que 'via est vobis, erit et mihi' … 'eadem'): the note calls 'vobis' and 'mihi' datives of possession, which holds whether 'qua … via' and 'eadem' are read as ablatives of route ('by whatever road') or as nominatives ('whatever road is yours'). The shipped literal leans ablative and the note's paraphrase leans nominative. Review judged both readings genuinely open and left the wording alone; a ratification pass should pick one.

House-rendering candidate, V.333 ('poscimur Aonides'): shipped as literal 'we Aonides are called for' and idiomatic 'then we of Aonia were called on'. A much-discussed half-line; recording the rendering so it is not re-decided.

V.290 typography: the edition prints the enclitic outside the quotation marks — “qua” que “via est vobis, erit et mihi” dixit “eadem” — so the tokenizer sees 'qua' and 'que' as two words where the grammar has one, 'quaque'. Shipped unaltered with an explanatory note. This looks like Magnus's own device rather than digitization damage, but it is worth a second pair of eyes in case the archive has split a word.

V.314 variant: Magnus prints 'cedamus' (hortatory subjunctive, 'let us withdraw'); the second witness reads 'cedemus' (future, 'we shall withdraw'). Mentioned in one clause in the note because the mood changes the force of the offer, not just the spelling. Confirm that is the right threshold.
V.262 variant (Magnus 'et', second witness 'est') was deliberately NOT noted: with 'et' the copula is simply understood and the sense is identical either way. Confirm.

Advisory call: trigger 2 fired on V.287–288 and the advisory is in object form. Trigger 3 was considered for V.292–293 (a man falling face-first from a tower, the bones of his face shattered, beating the ground as he dies) and ruled out on the length test — a line and a half, with the poem moving straight on. Flagging because it is the kind of case the length ruling was written for.

V.307 'venit': rendered as a historic present ('comes here') because the neighbouring 'committit' is present, but in an edition that marks no vowel lengths it could equally be the perfect 'vēnit'. The note says so; confirm the reading.

Hostile register, V.300 and V.305: 'istae' and 'stolidarum' are the narrating Muse's words for her rivals, not the poem's. 'stolidarum' is rendered 'stupid' and 'istae' is rendered with a demonstrative that keeps its distance, with the notes saying whose words they are. Check the level.

Review settled, for the record: the V.262 variant (Magnus 'et' / second witness 'est') is correctly left unnoted, since the sense is identical either way; the V.314 variant ('cedamus' / 'cedemus') is correctly noted, since mood changes the force of the offer; the advisory is correctly object-form on V.287–288 with graphic detail correctly declined at V.292–293 on the length test; and V.290 is the edition's own typography, not digitization damage — the line scans as a full hexameter with 'dixit' in place, so nothing has been split by the archive.
